newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold-Demand takes palpable hit on palladium.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold-Demand takes palpable hit on palladium.

text.p: Gold demand in Asia has taken a palpable hit as strong platinum and palladium prices pushed up gold prices and discouraged most buyers, bullion traders in Hong Kong and Singapore said on Friday.
"Physical demand remains pretty weak for the time being because the gold price managed to move by a few dollars and discouraged buyers," said a senior bullion trader in Hong Kong.
Gold and silver prices got support from this week's surge in platinum group metals prices due to continued disruption of Russian supplies and the brief strike at South Africa's Rustenberg mine.
Bullion traders in Asia said that price-sensitive gold demand would continue to depend on platinum and palladium.

"If they (platinum and palladium) are more stable, then gold will drift lower. If not, then we will follow the white metals," another Hong Kong source said, noting that gold could test US$348-$350 per ounce.
The strong rally in palladium prices this week to 17-year highs spilled over into gold, but any spike in Asian prices was likely be limited, Singapore dealers said.
"We're beginning to see some sympathy spilling over into gold. But I don't think we'll see too much followthrough," a senior dealer for a foreign bank in Singapore said.
Some gold traders said that other factors like softer economies and elections in Asia had also hit demand.

"Demand is quite weak at the moment. Indonesian buyers are sidelined because of the election. Thai buying has dried up due to its weak economy. In fact, all over Southeast Asia, gold demand has slipped because of the economic problems in the area," a Singapore bank trader said.
While physical demand was poor, stronger gold prices had attracted Australian producer selling, Singapore and Hong Kong sources said.
Hong Kong spot gold opened at $345.40/90 per ounce on Friday and had dropped to $345.10/60 per ounce by 0430 GMT, partially on Australian producer sales, dealers said.
"We saw some Australian selling at close to $346 per ounce, but gold is well supported at $345 because platinum remains pretty strong," one trader said.
Dealers said they were watching South Africa closely for news in the aftermath of the wildcat strike.

Gold demand across Asia would continue to slow down over the short term due to high prices, with steady buying by India providing the only glimmer of optimism in the region in the last week, dealers said.
"It's steady from the subcontinent but it's beginning to drop off," one dealer said. "Asian trade is pretty quiet right now."
One trader said there was lingering concern in the market over the German government's plan to overrule the Bundesbank and revalue its gold reserves to help Bonn qualify for Europe's single currency.
"There still some small concern about the German gold reserves, but we're waiting to see how it will play out," one Singapore trader said.
The market was also keeping a wary eye on foreign currency movements. "You have to keep an eye on the yen in case something comes up," one dealer said.
Singapore premiums were slightly easier at 80-90 U.S. cents over spot London prices from 80-100 cents last week, traders said.
